title: Speaking, Argument and Debate
description: Build arguments you can defend, take other people's apart fairly, and say it all out loud: structure, delivery, hard questions, persuasion and formal debate.
audience: A capable adult who reads and writes well and wants to argue and speak with more clarity and confidence. Has met logic (validity, fallacies) and rhetoric (claim, grounds, warrant; ethos, pathos, logos, kairos) on paper and now wants to use them live. A phone to record practice is helpful.
outcomes: You'll be able to reconstruct a speaker's argument and find its weakest link.
You'll be able to spot and answer common fallacies in real time without name-calling.
You'll be able to read percentages, risks and denominators correctly in a claim.
You'll be able to state the strongest version of a view you reject before you rebut it.
You'll be able to answer a question out loud in a clear structure and time it to the minute.
You'll be able to manage pace, fillers and nerves with measurable practice.
You'll be able to hold your message under hard questions without dodging.
You'll be able to follow the roles and rules of British Parliamentary debate and weigh competing impacts.

modules.title: Building and testing arguments
modules.summary: Hearing an argument as claim, reasons and evidence, and finding where it can be attacked fairly.

modules.title: Speaking clearly
modules.summary: The structure of a spoken answer, delivery you can measure, and holding your message under pressure.

modules.title: Persuasion
modules.summary: Audience, credibility, story, framing, and where persuasion becomes manipulation.

modules.title: Debate
modules.summary: A formal format with roles and time limits, and the work of building and weighing a case.

lessons.title: Hearing an argument
lessons.objective: Reconstruct a speaker's claim, reasons and evidence from a short speech and separate them from assertion and explanation.

concepts.title: Claim
concepts.summary: A claim is the statement the speaker wants you to accept.

concepts.title: Reason
concepts.summary: A reason is a statement offered as a ground for believing the claim.

concepts.title: Evidence
concepts.summary: Evidence is a fact, example, statistic or testimony that supports a reason.

concepts.title: Explanation and argument
concepts.summary: An explanation says why something is so when both sides already accept it; an argument tries to make someone accept a claim that is in doubt.

concepts.title: Argument signposts
concepts.summary: Words such as 'because', 'so' and 'therefore' mark a reason or a conclusion, though many arguments have none.

misconceptions: Thinking an argument is a quarrel: here it means offering reasons for a claim, calmly.
Thinking a strong opinion is evidence: confidence and repetition are delivery, not support.
Taking the first sentence as the claim: speakers often put the claim last, or never state it.
sequence: Play a one-minute speech and ask the listener to say the claim in one sentence.
Separate the reasons from the claim, and the evidence from the reasons.
Show how listeners hear arguments differently from readers: they cannot reread, so speakers repeat and signpost.
Distinguish explanation from argument using a pair of near-identical paragraphs.
Recap with a standard-form summary: claim, reason 1 with evidence, reason 2 with evidence.
examples: Speech: 'We should stop the 8 a.m. meeting. People are tired at that hour, and our own survey found 14 of 20 staff prefer 10 a.m.' Claim: stop the 8 a.m. meeting. Reasons: people are tired; staff prefer 10 a.m. Evidence: 14 of 20.
Explanation: 'The pub is closed because the owner is ill.' Argument: 'The pub is probably closed because the lights are off and the door is locked.'
A claim placed last: 'Hours are cut, prices are up and the town is empty. The mall must go.'

figures.shows: A short speech transcript on the left and a blank claim/reasons/evidence frame on the right.
figures.learnerAction: Drag sentences into the frame.

figures.shows: Two paragraphs, one explanation and one argument, side by side.
figures.learnerAction: Mark which is which.

questionPlan.sample: 'Hours are cut, prices are up and the town is empty. The mall must go.' What is the claim?
Which of these is evidence for 'staff prefer 10 a.m.'?
questionPlan.answer: 14 of 20 staff chose 10 a.m. in the survey.
choices: 14 of 20 staff chose 10 a.m. in the survey.
The manager feels strongly about it.

questionPlan.sample: What word names a statement offered as a ground for believing a claim?

lessons.title: Finding the weak link
lessons.objective: Use claim, grounds, warrant, qualifier and rebuttal to decide where an argument can be questioned, and ask two or three short questions that expose it.

concepts.title: Attacking grounds
concepts.summary: You can ask whether the facts offered are true, current and complete.

concepts.title: Attacking the warrant
concepts.summary: You can ask whether the facts, even if true, really support the claim; the warrant is the general rule that links them.

concepts.title: Qualifier
concepts.summary: A qualifier such as 'probably' or 'in most cases' sets the strength the speaker claims, and a strong claim with weak support is easy to push on.

concepts.title: Exception
concepts.summary: An exception, or rebuttal in Toulmin's term, is a condition under which the warrant fails.

concepts.title: Closed question
concepts.summary: A short yes-or-no question exposes a weak link by making the speaker commit, and is most useful when you already know the likely answer.

misconceptions: Attacking the conclusion directly: 'You're wrong' gives the speaker nothing to answer. A better attack names the grounds or the warrant.
Treating every argument as weak because it has exceptions: a qualified argument already allows for them. The question is whether the exception applies here.
Thinking questions must be hostile: the best ones are short, neutral and fair.
sequence: Recall claim, grounds and warrant from the English course and add the qualifier and the exception.

Use Toulmin's example: 'Harry was born in Bermuda, so presumably he is a British subject.' The warrant is that a man born in Bermuda will generally be a British subject; the exception is that his parents were aliens.
Show three attack points: the grounds, the warrant, the exception, and ask which fits a given argument.
Write two closed questions that expose the weak link.
Practise on a recorded 90-second argument by someone else: say the weak link aloud.
examples: Toulmin: claim 'Harry is a British subject'; grounds 'Harry was born in Bermuda'; warrant 'A man born in Bermuda will generally be a British subject'; qualifier 'presumably'; exception 'both his parents were aliens'.
'Everyone at the gym is fit, so the gym makes you fit.' The warrant (those who attend are fit because of the gym) ignores that fit people join gyms.
Closed question: 'Did the survey ask people who do not use the gym?'

figures.shows: A Toulmin layout with boxes for claim, grounds, warrant, qualifier and exception for a short argument; one box is left empty.
figures.learnerAction: Drag the missing part into the empty box, then pick which box to attack.

figures.shows: A short transcript with sentences that can be clicked.
figures.learnerAction: Click the sentence you would question first (answer revealed afterward).

questionPlan.sample: 'Harry was born in Bermuda, so presumably he is a British subject.' Which part is the warrant?
questionPlan.answer: A man born in Bermuda will generally be a British subject.
choices: A man born in Bermuda will generally be a British subject.

questionPlan.sample: What is the word 'presumably' called in Toulmin's model?
Which fact would be an exception to the Harry warrant?
questionPlan.answer: Both of Harry's parents were aliens.
choices: Harry was born in a hospital.
Both of Harry's parents were aliens.

historyNotes: Stephen Toulmin published The Uses of Argument in 1958, where he used the Bermuda example.

lessons.title: Fallacies at speed
lessons.objective: Recognise common fallacies as they are spoken and reply without name-calling, and avoid the mistake of treating a fallacy as proof that the conclusion is false.

concepts.title: Ad hominem
concepts.summary: An ad hominem attack answers the person instead of the argument.

concepts.title: Straw man
concepts.summary: A straw man attacks a weaker, distorted version of the other side's view.

concepts.title: False dilemma
concepts.summary: A false dilemma presents two options as the only ones when others exist.

concepts.title: Hasty generalisation
concepts.summary: A hasty generalisation draws a broad conclusion from too few or unrepresentative cases.

concepts.title: The fallacy fallacy
concepts.summary: Concluding that a claim is false because someone argued for it badly is itself an error: the claim may be true with other support.

concepts.title: Name and redirect
concepts.summary: A calm reply restates what was done and returns to the argument: 'That's about me, not the plan. Can we look at the cost figure?'

misconceptions: Treating the label as a win: calling 'straw man!' without saying how the version differs only changes the topic.
Thinking every appeal to authority is a fallacy: citing a relevant expert is reasonable, and the fallacy is citing someone outside their field or only their fame.
Thinking that spotting a fallacy refutes the conclusion: it only removes that support.
sequence: Recall the fallacies named in the logic course and hear them in short spoken examples.
Show a spoken reply for each: say what the move was and what you want back.
Discuss the fallacy fallacy with a true claim supported by a bad argument.
Cover appeal to authority and its legitimate form.
Practise: listen to a recorded clip and name the move in a sentence.
examples: 'You can't trust his tax plan; he has been divorced twice.' (ad hominem)
'Either we ban all cars or we accept filthy air.' (false dilemma)
'Both my neighbours had the flu jab and got sick, so jabs make you ill.' (hasty generalisation, two cases)

figures.shows: Six spoken examples in one column and six fallacy names in another.
figures.learnerAction: Match each example to its fallacy.

figures.shows: A short dialogue with a response box beneath each line.
figures.learnerAction: Pick the best calm redirect from three options.

questionPlan.sample: 'You can't trust his tax plan; he has been divorced twice.' Which fallacy is this?
'Either we ban all cars or we accept filthy air.' Which fallacy is this?
Someone gives a bad argument for a claim. What can you conclude about the claim?
questionPlan.answer: nothing yet: it may still be true on other grounds
choices: nothing yet: it may still be true on other grounds

lessons.title: Numbers in argument
lessons.objective: Read relative and absolute change, percentages and percentage points, and ask the one question that checks a statistic: compared with what?

concepts.title: Absolute and relative change
concepts.summary: Absolute change is the difference between two numbers; relative change is that difference as a fraction of the starting number.

concepts.title: Percentage point
concepts.summary: A percentage point is the difference between two percentages, which is not the same as a percent change.

concepts.title: Denominator
concepts.summary: The denominator says what the count is a fraction of, and a number without one cannot be judged.

concepts.title: Sample size and selection
concepts.summary: A claim from few or self-selected cases is weaker than the same claim from many random ones.

concepts.title: Compared with what
concepts.summary: Most misleading statistics leave out the comparison, such as the base rate or the other group.

misconceptions: Treating '50 percent' as large without asking 50 percent of what: a 50 percent rise from 2 in 1,000 to 3 in 1,000 is 1 extra case in 1,000.
Mixing up percent and percentage points: a rise from 4 percent to 5 percent is 1 percentage point, or 25 percent in relative terms.
Trusting a vivid number with no denominator: 'Six people were hurt' means little without the number who used it.
sequence: Show a headline claim: 'risk doubled'. Ask two questions: from what, and to what?
Define absolute and relative change and compute both for the same figures.
Separate percent from percentage points.
Add denominators and base rates.
Close with how to say it in a speech: give both the relative and absolute figures.
examples: Risk goes from 2 in 1,000 to 3 in 1,000: relative change 50 percent; absolute change 0.1 percentage points (0.3 percent minus 0.2 percent).
Unemployment goes from 4 percent to 5 percent: 1 percentage point; relative change 25 percent.
A drug 'cuts risk by 50 percent' from 2 in 1,000 to 1 in 1,000: absolute reduction 0.1 percentage points.

figures.shows: Two bar charts of the same data, one with absolute axis starting at zero and one with a truncated axis.
figures.learnerAction: Toggle between the axes.

figures.shows: A grid of 'before' and 'after' values with columns for absolute change, relative change and percentage points.
figures.learnerAction: Complete the columns for each row.

questionPlan.sample: A treatment lowers risk from 2 in 1,000 to 1 in 1,000. By how many percentage points does the risk fall?
Unemployment rises from 4 percent to 5 percent. By what percent, relative to the starting figure, has it risen?
'Six people were hurt on the new slide.' What do you most need to know to judge this?
questionPlan.answer: how many people used the slide
choices: how many people used the slide

lessons.title: Steelman and rebuttal
lessons.objective: State the strongest fair version of a view you disagree with and answer it with a structured rebuttal.

concepts.title: Steelman
concepts.summary: A steelman is the strongest version of the other side's case, stated so that its supporters would accept it.

concepts.title: Rapoport's rules
concepts.summary: State the other view so fairly that its holder would say 'I wish I'd put it that way'; list your agreements; say what you have learned; only then rebut.

concepts.title: Rebuttal moves
concepts.summary: A rebuttal can deny the evidence, deny the link between evidence and claim, give an exception, or concede and show that your side outweighs it.

concepts.title: Burden of proof
concepts.summary: The burden of proof lies on whoever makes the claim, and it rises with the strength and surprise of the claim.

concepts.title: Concession
concepts.summary: Conceding a point you cannot defend gains credibility and lets you argue from a position of strength.

misconceptions: Thinking fairness weakens your side: stating the other view well makes your reply harder to dismiss.
Thinking a rebuttal must win every point: choose the point that decides the case and let the rest go.
Thinking 'prove me wrong' shifts the burden: the claimant carries it.
sequence: Take a short speech and write its strongest version in five sentences.
Introduce Dennett's retelling of Rapoport's four rules.
Match rebuttal moves to a given weak link from the earlier lesson.
Explain burden of proof with a claim and a counter-claim.
Practise: record a 2-minute rebuttal that begins with a fair restatement.
examples: Rapoport's rules (Dennett, 2013): restate fairly; list agreements; say what you learned; then rebut.
A claim 'the plan will cut commuting time' met by 'the evidence is from one week in August' (deny the evidence).
A rebuttal that concedes: 'It will cost more, and it saves lives; I'd argue lives outweigh cost.'

figures.shows: A speech summary and four rebuttal cards.
figures.learnerAction: Choose which card targets the weakest part; the card's explanation appears afterward.

figures.shows: Rapoport's four rules as a checklist with space for the learner's restatement.
figures.learnerAction: Write a five-sentence restatement and tick the rules met.

questionPlan.sample: What do we call attacking a weaker, distorted version of the other side's view?
A speaker's evidence comes from a single week in August. Which rebuttal move fits best?
Write the strongest five-sentence version of a view you reject. Rate whether someone who holds it would sign off on it.

historyNotes: Anatol Rapoport's rules for criticism were popularised by Daniel Dennett in Intuition Pumps (2013).

lessons.title: The structure of a spoken answer
lessons.objective: Answer any question aloud in a clear four-part structure, with signposts, inside a set time.

concepts.title: PREP
concepts.summary: PREP is Point, Reason, Example, Point: answer first, give why, give a case, then restate.

concepts.title: Signposting
concepts.summary: Signposts such as 'first', 'second' and 'so' tell listeners where they are.

concepts.title: Rule of three
concepts.summary: Three points are usually enough to feel complete and few enough to remember.

concepts.title: Speaking time
concepts.summary: At about 150 words a minute, a minute of speech is about 150 words.

concepts.title: Spoken versus written
concepts.summary: Listeners cannot reread, so speech uses shorter sentences, repetition and explicit structure.

misconceptions: Building up to the answer: listeners should hear the point first because they cannot skim ahead.
Adding more points to seem thorough: past three, listeners drop earlier ones.
Reading aloud writing designed for the eye: long subordinate sentences lose a listener.
sequence: Ask a question and answer it twice, once wandering and once with PREP.
Define PREP and signposting.
Plan time: 150 words per minute and thirty-second slots.
Compare spoken and written style with two versions of one paragraph.
Practise: answer three random questions in 60 to 90 seconds each, recorded and self-rated.
examples: Question: 'Should we move to a four-day week?' Point: yes. Reason: output holds up. Example: a named trial. Point: so I'd pilot it.
A 2-minute answer: 15 s opening, three points of 30 s each, 15 s close.
A 90-second answer at 150 words per minute is about 225 words.

figures.shows: A timeline bar of a 2-minute answer with slots for opening, three points and close.
figures.learnerAction: Drag boundaries to allocate time; totals update.

figures.shows: A PREP template with sample questions.
figures.learnerAction: Fill the four lines for a chosen question.

questionPlan.sample: In the PREP pattern, what does the P at the end of the answer stand for?
A 2-minute answer uses a 15-second opening, a 15-second close and three equal points. How many seconds does each point get?
At 150 words a minute, about how many words is a 90-second answer?

lessons.title: Voice, pace and nerves
lessons.objective: Measure your pace and fillers from a recording, set one thing to change, and use nerves as energy.

concepts.title: Pace
concepts.summary: Pace is words per minute; conversational speech is commonly 120 to 170 words a minute, and slower is often clearer in a large room.

concepts.title: Pause
concepts.summary: A pause marks a point, gives listeners time to take it in, and replaces filler.

concepts.title: Filler rate
concepts.summary: Filler rate is the number of 'um', 'like' and similar words per minute.

concepts.title: Projection and articulation
concepts.summary: Projection is volume carried by breath, and articulation is the clear formation of consonants.

concepts.title: Reappraising nerves
concepts.summary: Describing nervous arousal as excitement rather than trying to calm down improved performance in studies by Alison Wood Brooks (2014).

misconceptions: Believing the goal is to remove every filler: the goal is to replace the habitual ones with silence where it helps.
Believing speaking faster shows confidence: rushing tends to flatten emphasis and signals nerves.
Believing you should calm down first: telling yourself to be excited can work better than telling yourself to calm down.
sequence: Record a 60-second talk and play it back.
Count words, time and fillers; compute pace and filler rate.
Set one target (pace, pause or filler) and rerun.
Explain projection and articulation with one tongue-twister drill.
Present reappraisal as one tool and say how much evidence stands behind it.
examples: A 450-word talk of 3 minutes: 450 / 3 = 150 words a minute.
18 fillers in 3 minutes: 18 / 3 = 6 a minute.
A 7-minute speech at 140 words a minute is about 980 words.

figures.shows: A line chart of words per minute across five recordings, with the target band 120 to 160 shaded.
figures.learnerAction: Enter a count and time for a new recording.

figures.shows: A practice log with columns for date, words, minutes, fillers, one change.
figures.learnerAction: Add a row after each recording.

questionPlan.sample: A recording has 450 words and lasts 3 minutes. What is the pace in words per minute?
A talk of 3 minutes contains 18 fillers. How many fillers per minute is that?
Record a 60-second talk, count your fillers, and replace the most common one with a pause. Rate the second recording against the first.

historyNotes: Alison Wood Brooks published 'Get excited: reappraising pre-performance anxiety as excitement' in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: General in 2014.

lessons.title: Questions and staying on message
lessons.objective: Answer hard questions by acknowledging, bridging and returning to a key message, without dodging a direct factual question.

concepts.title: Key message
concepts.summary: A key message is the one thing you want the listener to remember, in about 20 words or fewer.

concepts.title: Acknowledge, Bridge, Communicate
concepts.summary: ABC answers the question asked, bridges with a short phrase, then says the message.

concepts.title: Hostile framing
concepts.summary: A hostile question may contain a loaded premise; you can restate the question in neutral terms before answering.

concepts.title: Saying you do not know
concepts.summary: Saying 'I don't know, and here is how I'll find out' is honest and sustains credibility.

concepts.title: Direct questions
concepts.summary: A direct yes-or-no question about a fact deserves a direct answer before any bridge.

misconceptions: Treating a bridge as a way to avoid answering: a bridge works only after a real answer.
Repeating the negative framing in the answer: it carries the loaded premise into your own voice.
Treating 'no comment' as neutral: listeners hear it as concealment.
sequence: Take a hostile question and write your key message in 20 words.
Walk through ABC on it.
Show a bad bridge that dodges and a good one that answers first.
Practise: ask six tough questions about your own claim and answer each aloud in 30 seconds.
Review: did you answer the question, bridge once, and say the message?
examples: Q: 'Isn't this just a way to cut jobs?' A: 'People worry about that, and no one loses their job under this plan. What matters is that the service stays open at weekends.'
Key message: 'The weekend service stays open and nobody loses a job.' (11 words)
A direct question: 'Did it happen?' needs 'Yes' or 'No' first.

figures.shows: Three answer cards per question, one that dodges, one that answers and bridges, one that repeats the loaded premise.
figures.learnerAction: Choose the best card; each is explained afterwards.

figures.shows: ABC template with space for acknowledge, bridge and message.
figures.learnerAction: Fill the template for three questions.

questionPlan.sample: In the ABC method, what does B stand for?
A key message should be about how many words or fewer?
Record yourself answering six tough questions about your own view in 30 seconds each. Rate whether each answer addressed the question before bridging.

lessons.title: Audience, credibility and story
lessons.objective: Adapt a talk to a specific audience, build credibility on purpose, and use a story as evidence instead of decoration.

concepts.title: Audience analysis
concepts.summary: Audience analysis asks what the listeners know, want and fear, and what they will do after hearing you.

concepts.title: Building credibility
concepts.summary: Credibility comes from competence, goodwill and character, and is shown more by preparation, fairness and honesty than by claims about yourself.

concepts.title: Story as evidence
concepts.summary: A story works as evidence when it is representative and tied to the claim, and as decoration when it is not.

concepts.title: Contrast arc
concepts.summary: Many persuasive talks alternate 'what is' with 'what could be', building movement toward a call to action.

concepts.title: Call to action
concepts.summary: A call to action says exactly what the audience should do next, by when.

misconceptions: Believing the best talk persuades everyone: the same talk to a technical and a general audience should differ in vocabulary, order and proof.
Opening with credentials: listeners judge credibility from how you treat them and the evidence.
Using a moving story that does not represent the cases: it persuades by emotion, not by support.
sequence: Pose two audiences for one claim and ask what each needs.
Recall ethos, pathos, logos and kairos from the English course and say which an audience needs more of.
Show credibility as preparation and fairness, with examples.
Show a story used as evidence and a story used as decoration.
Outline a two-minute pitch with a call to action and record it.
examples: Claim: 'Staff should use AI tools for drafts.' To a manager: cost and risk. To staff: time saved and rules.
A story about one customer that stands for 400 similar complaints is representative; a single unusual case is not.
Call to action: 'Approve the 3-month trial at Monday's meeting.'

figures.shows: Two audience profiles with columns for what they know, want, and fear, and a talk outline between them.
figures.learnerAction: Reorder outline blocks for each audience.

figures.shows: A talk drawn as a line of 'what is' and 'what could be' alternations.
figures.learnerAction: Place story, evidence and call to action on the line.

questionPlan.sample: Which opening is best for a sceptical technical audience?
questionPlan.answer: a specific measurement and how it was taken
choices: a specific measurement and how it was taken

questionPlan.sample: A single unusual case is told as proof of a general claim. How is the story functioning?
Record a 2-minute pitch for a view of yours that ends in one specific call to action. Rate whether the audience would know exactly what to do next.

historyNotes: Aristotle's Rhetoric (4th century BC) names ethos, pathos and logos as the three means of persuasion by speech.

lessons.title: Framing and ethical persuasion
lessons.objective: Explain how framing and social-influence principles change responses to the same facts, and apply a simple test of whether a technique persuades or manipulates.

concepts.title: Framing effect
concepts.summary: The same outcomes described as gains or as losses can lead people to choose differently.

concepts.title: Expected value
concepts.summary: The expected value of a gamble is the sum of each outcome multiplied by its probability.

concepts.title: Influence principles
concepts.summary: Cialdini described reciprocity, commitment and consistency, social proof, authority, liking and scarcity (later adding unity) as common levers of compliance.

concepts.title: Persuasion and manipulation
concepts.summary: Persuasion gives the listener true information and reasons they can check; manipulation works by hiding or bypassing them.

concepts.title: Transparency test
concepts.summary: A technique passes if you would be comfortable with the listener seeing exactly how and why you used it.

misconceptions: Believing equal outcomes feel equal: 'saves 200' and 'lets 400 die' describe the same thing to different effect.
Believing all use of emotion is manipulation: emotion that fits the facts is part of honest persuasion.
Believing a technique is ethical because it works: the test is honesty and respect for the listener's judgment.
sequence: Present Tversky and Kahneman's 600-person problem in two frames with the same numbers.
Compute the expected number saved for each programme.
Name Cialdini's principles with one honest use and one abuse of each.
Define manipulation and give the transparency test.
Apply the test to three real persuasion scenarios.
examples: Programme A saves 200 of 600; Programme B has a one-third chance of saving all 600 and a two-thirds chance of saving none: expected saved = 600 x 1/3 = 200.
Scarcity: 'Only 3 seats left' is honest if true and manipulation if invented.
Social proof: 'Most of your neighbours pay on time' stated truthfully.

figures.shows: The two programmes drawn as outcomes with probabilities.
figures.learnerAction: Compute the expected number saved for each before the frames are shown.

figures.shows: Six influence principles with a column for an honest use and one for an abuse.
figures.learnerAction: Complete one honest use and one abuse for two principles.

questionPlan.sample: A programme has a one-in-three chance of saving all 600 people and a two-in-three chance of saving none. What is the expected number saved?
A seller says 'Only 3 left' when 40 are in stock. Which influence principle is being abused?
Which test best separates persuasion from manipulation?
questionPlan.answer: would you be comfortable with the listener seeing how and why you used the technique
choices: would you be comfortable with the listener seeing how and why you used the technique

historyNotes: Amos Tversky and Daniel Kahneman published the framing study in Science in 1981.

lessons.title: The British Parliamentary format
lessons.objective: Name the teams, speakers, times and rules of a British Parliamentary debate and say what each speaker must do.

concepts.title: Four teams
concepts.summary: A British Parliamentary debate has four teams of two: Opening Government, Opening Opposition, Closing Government and Closing Opposition.

concepts.title: Speaking order
concepts.summary: The eight speeches go in order: Prime Minister, Leader of the Opposition, Deputy Prime Minister, Deputy Leader of the Opposition, Member for the Government, Member for the Opposition, Government Whip, Opposition Whip.

concepts.title: Time and prep
concepts.summary: Each speech is 7 minutes, and teams receive the motion about 15 minutes before the round.

concepts.title: Point of information
concepts.summary: A point of information is a short interruption offered by the opposing side, allowed after the first minute and before the last minute of a speech.

concepts.title: Ranking
concepts.summary: The four teams are ranked first to fourth for 3, 2, 1 and 0 points; closing teams must add a new extension rather than repeat the opening teams.

misconceptions: Believing the closing teams just repeat and summarise: they must add a new extension and separate their case from the opening team's.
Believing the debate is two-sided: it is four teams in competition, and the closing team on your own side is also a rival.
Believing interruptions are rude: points of information are part of the format, offered briefly and answered or declined.
sequence: Draw the table with four teams and eight chairs.
Show speaking order and who is who.
State times: 7 minutes per speech, 15 minutes of prep.
Explain protected time for points of information (the first and last minute).
Explain team ranking and the extension requirement.
examples: Total speaking time: 8 speeches x 7 minutes = 56 minutes.
Points offered in a 7-minute speech: after minute 1 and before minute 6, a 5-minute window.
Points in a round: 3 + 2 + 1 + 0 = 6.

figures.learnerAction: Place the speaker names in the correct seats.

lessons.title: Building and weighing a case
lessons.objective: Analyse a motion, build arguments with a mechanism and an impact, and weigh competing impacts by magnitude, probability, timeframe and reversibility.

concepts.title: Motion analysis
concepts.summary: Motion analysis fixes what the motion asks, who the actors are and what each side must show.

concepts.title: Mechanism and impact
concepts.summary: An argument states a claim, explains the mechanism by which it happens and the impact that matters.

concepts.title: Weighing
concepts.summary: Weighing compares impacts by magnitude, probability, timeframe and reversibility, and says why yours matter more.

concepts.title: Extension
concepts.summary: An extension is a substantive new argument or analysis from a closing team.

concepts.title: Self-review
concepts.summary: Self-review scores a recorded speech against its role, its matter (content), its manner (delivery) and its use of time.

misconceptions: Thinking the larger impact always wins: a huge impact with low probability can lose to a modest, near-certain one.
Assuming the other side's impacts are zero: concede what is true and argue that yours weighs more.
Listing points without mechanisms: a claim with no explanation of how it happens is only an assertion.
sequence: Read a motion and write what each side must show in two sentences.
Build one argument: claim, mechanism, impact.
Compare two impacts using expected size: probability times number affected.
Add the other axes: timeframe and reversibility.
Record a 4-minute case and review it against the criteria.
examples: Impact A: helps 1,000 people with probability 0.3, expected 300. Impact B: helps 200 people with probability 0.9, expected 180. A outweighs B on expected size.
Weighing sentence: 'Even if the other side is right about cost, ours is larger, more likely and cannot be undone.'
Extension: a new group of people affected that the opening bench did not mention.

figures.shows: Two impacts with numbers and probabilities.
figures.learnerAction: Compute the expected size of each before weighing.

questionPlan.sample: Impact A helps 1,000 people with probability 0.3. What is the expected number helped?
Impact B helps 200 people with probability 0.9. What is the expected number helped?
Record a 4-minute case for a motion and score it 1 to 5 on role, matter, manner and time.

historyNotes: The matter, manner and method scoring used by some debating bodies (such as the Australasian format) differs from the BP criteria; the lesson should follow the manual cited for the course.

courseCheck: A mixed check of: extracting claim, reasons and evidence from a short speech; locating the warrant and an exception; naming common fallacies and the fallacy fallacy; computing absolute and relative change and percentage points; choosing a rebuttal move; allotting time in a spoken answer and computing pace and filler rate; completing the ABC steps; computing an expected value in a framed problem; stating the British Parliamentary roles, times and points window; and weighing two numerical impacts. Practice recordings are self-rated.
platformNeeds: Audio recording and playback inside a self-rated practice task: record, play back, show a timer and a word or filler counter the learner fills in, and save the rating. The recording should stay on the device (no upload) unless the learner chooses otherwise. Until then the 'self' question kind with a phone recording works and the practice log is a 'table' figure.
Timed speaking prompts: a countdown, a random-question generator from a curated list, and a speech-time bar (for the BP lesson). svg_figure and timeline_explorer fallbacks stand in.

A 'transcript_annotation' figure: select spans of a short transcript and label them (claim, reason, evidence, warrant, exception, fallacy). A clickable svg_figure with preset sentences is the fallback.
Optional: a debate round simulator that plays pre-written speeches and lets the learner decide where to raise a point of information. Not required.
unverified: All external source URLs: the research session had no outbound web access, so none were opened, and the licence for each (UNC handouts CC BY-NC-ND 4.0, Stand Up Speak Out CC BY-NC-SA 3.0, CDC public domain) was written from memory. The WUDC manual's licence was not found.

The WUDC details (7-minute speeches, 15 minutes of preparation, points of information allowed after the first minute and before the last, 3-2-1-0 team points, the extension requirement and the eight speaker titles) are from memory of the manual; the lesson writer must read the current manual before writing.
Toulmin's Bermuda example is paraphrased from memory of The Uses of Argument (1958); check the exact warrant and rebuttal wording.
The Brooks (2014) reappraisal study, Tversky and Kahneman (1981), Cialdini's list including the later 'unity' principle and the Rapoport rules as given by Dennett (2013) are from memory.
The 120 to 170 words per minute range for conversational speech and the 150 words per minute figure are rules of thumb; the 150 value is used only for arithmetic.

Overlap with existing courses: the English course already has 'Claim, grounds and warrant' and 'Ethos, pathos, logos and kairos', and the logic course has 'Naming the fallacies'. This plan was checked against lesson titles only. The lessons here reuse those ideas for live use, but a writer should read those lessons and trim repeated material.
The matter, manner and method criteria attributed to Australasian debating are from memory.
